final_proof:
Let \(X\) be a set and let \(\mathcal A\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\). Thus \(X\in\mathcal A\), \(X\setminus E\in\mathcal A\) for every \(E\in\mathcal A\), and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\mathcal A\) for every sequence \((E_n)_{n\geq1}\) of members of \(\mathcal A\).

By complement closure, \(\varnothing=X\setminus X\in\mathcal A\). Now take arbitrary \(A,B\in\mathcal A\), and define a sequence by \(E_1=A\), \(E_2=B\), and \(E_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\geq3\). Every \(E_n\) belongs to \(\mathcal A\). Therefore countable-union closure yields
\[
A\cup B=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\mathcal A.
\]
Thus set union is closed on \(\mathcal A\); equivalently, its restriction is a map \(\cup:\mathcal A\times\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\).

A magma is a nonempty set equipped with an internal binary operation. Since \(X\in\mathcal A\), the family \(\mathcal A\) is nonempty; since \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(X)\), all its elements are sets; and the preceding argument shows that union is an internal binary operation on it. Hence \((\mathcal A,\cup)\) is a magma of sets, as claimed.
